title: Glossary
markdown:
Terms from the lessons written so far, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is given in brackets.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Access violation** | The error Windows raises when a program reads or writes memory it is not allowed to touch, such as address 0. It stops the program. (1.03) |
| **Address** | The number of a byte in memory. A variable's address is the number of its first byte. Written in hexadecimal. (1.03) |
| **Address space layout randomisation** | A Windows security feature that loads programs at a different place in memory on each run. (1.03) |
| **Alignment** | The rule that a value should start at an address that is a multiple of its size, because the processor reads it fastest there. (1.03) |
| **Base plus offset** | Describing a location as "where something starts this time" plus a fixed distance, because absolute addresses change between runs. (1.03) |
| **Binary** | Base 2. Numbers written with only the digits 0 and 1. (1.02) |
| **Bit** | One binary digit: a switch that is on or off. (1.02) |
| **Byte** | Eight bits. The unit that memory is measured and numbered in. (1.02) |
| **Compiler** | The program that translates C++ into the processor's own instructions. (1.01) |
| **CPU** | The processor: the part that carries out instructions. (1.01) |
| **Decode** | The step of the cycle in which the CPU works out what a fetched instruction means. (1.01) |
| **Dereference** | To go to the address a pointer holds and use the value there. Written `*p`. (1.03) |
| **Execute** | The step of the cycle in which the CPU carries out an instruction. (1.01) |
| **Fetch** | The step of the cycle in which the CPU copies the next instruction out of memory. (1.01) |
| **Heap** | The region of memory a program asks for while it runs. (1.03) |
| **Hexadecimal** | Base 16, with the digits 0 to 9 and A to F. One hex digit is exactly four bits. Written with `0x` in front. (1.02) |
| **Instruction register** | The register that holds the instruction the CPU is currently working on. (1.01) |
| **Little-endian** | A byte order in which the lowest-value byte of a number is stored at the lowest address. PCs use it. (1.02) |
| **Memory (RAM)** | Where a running program and the values it is using are held. Emptied when the power goes off. (1.01) |
| **Null pointer** | A pointer holding address 0, meaning it is not aimed at anything. Written `nullptr`. (1.03) |
| **Overflow** | Going past the largest value a type can hold. Unsigned values wrap round to zero. (1.02) |
| **Padding** | Unused bytes the compiler leaves between values to keep them aligned. (1.03) |
| **Pointer** | A variable whose value is an address. (1.03) |
| **Pointer arithmetic** | Adding to or subtracting from a pointer. It moves by whole elements, not single bytes. (1.03) |
| **Process** | A program that has been loaded into memory and is running. (1.01) |
| **Program counter** | The register that holds the address of the next instruction to fetch. (1.01) |
| **Register** | A small, very fast storage slot inside the CPU. (1.01) |
| **Stack** | The region of memory that holds the local variables of functions that are currently running. (1.03) |
| **Storage** | Disks and SSDs: where files are kept for the long term. (1.01) |
| **Two's complement** | The way negative whole numbers are stored: the top bit is worth minus its usual amount. (1.02) |
| **Undefined behaviour** | Something the C++ language makes no promise about. The program may crash, misbehave, or appear to work. (1.02, 1.03) |
